analysis.one_liner: Requires hospitals and nursing homes to publish nurse staffing levels and patient safety outcomes.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a House vote — it died in a subcommittee with all 19 of its House supporters being Democrats.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made Medicare providers — hospitals, psychiatric hospitals, rural clinics, surgical centers, and dialysis facilities — publish how many nurses they staff on each unit and shift, along with patient death rates and records of errors and infections. Nursing homes would have had to submit quarterly staffing data that gets audited and posted online so families could compare facilities. It also would have made it illegal for providers to fire or punish employees who report dangerous conditions, with fines up to $20,000 per violation.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and families choosing a hospital or nursing home would get hard numbers on nurse staffing, mortality, infections, medication errors, and pressure sores — and on complaints and inspection findings — instead of marketing claims. Nurses and other hospital employees would gain legal protection against being fired or demoted for reporting dangerous conditions. The bill's stated logic, citing research it says shows a 7% jump in patient death odds for every extra patient added to a nurse's workload, is that public disclosure would pressure facilities to staff adequately.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hospital and nursing home patients, and nurses

how_it_helps.text: Medicare providers — hospitals, psychiatric hospitals, rural health clinics, ambulatory surgical centers, and dialysis facilities — would have to publicly report registered nurse and licensed practical nurse counts, unlicensed aide numbers, and average patients per nurse, broken down by unit and shift, as a condition of staying in Medicare.
Providers would have to publish risk-adjusted patient mortality rates and adverse incidents including medication errors, patient injuries, pressure ulcers, and hospital-acquired infections.

Nursing homes would submit staffing data electronically every quarter, the data would be audited during standard inspections, and the government would post a staffing quality measure showing each facility's percentile ranking in its state and its nurse retention rates.
Complaints filed with state agencies, CMS, or accrediting bodies — plus investigation findings and scheduled inspection results — would be made publicly available.
Providers could not fire, demote, or otherwise punish employees for reporting conditions dangerous to patients or staff, with civil money penalties of up to $20,000 per retaliatory action.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, nursing homes, and other Medicare providers would bear the cost of collecting and electronically submitting detailed staffing data every quarter, of inspections that now include data audits, and of reputational exposure from public mortality and incident rankings. Providers that retaliate against whistleblowing employees would face civil fines of up to $20,000 per action. Small providers could get a waiver if reporting would be unduly burdensome.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hospitals, nursing homes, and dialysis facilities

drawbacks.text: The bill is a transparency measure, not a staffing mandate: it requires disclosure but sets no minimum nurse-to-patient ratio, so an understaffed facility could comply simply by publishing its own poor numbers.

Public mortality and complication rankings depend on risk adjustment, which is imperfect, so consumers comparing facilities on a website could be misled by numbers that don't fully account for how sick each facility's patients were.
The $20,000-per-violation cap on penalties for retaliating against a whistleblowing employee is small relative to the revenues of large hospital systems, limiting the deterrent.
Quarterly electronic reporting by unit and shift is a real paperwork burden for providers, which the bill itself acknowledges by allowing the Secretary to waive requirements for small providers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is real but indirect: the bill gives patients and families better information and gives nurses protection to speak up, betting that market and regulatory pressure will push facilities toward adequate staffing, citing research in its own findings that staffing levels affect patient deaths. The costs — quarterly data reporting and audit exposure — are modest for large providers, and the penalties for retaliation are weak. On balance it is a low-cost, useful disclosure bill, but it would not itself have forced any facility to hire another nurse.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to two House committees, then to a Health Subcommittee, and sat there until the Congress ended — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Maurice Hinchey introduced the Patient Safety Act of 2005 in the House with 14 original cosponsors on November 16, 2005.
The Speaker referred it to the Ways and Means Committee and, for the provisions in its jurisdiction, to the Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced.
On December 2, 2005, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, and the record shows no further action for the rest of the 109th Congress, which ended January 3, 2007.
The bill gathered 18 cosponsors, all Democrats, and never reached a floor vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospital and nursing home operators are better off because the bill died: they avoided mandatory public reporting of staffing, mortality, and complaint data, and avoided a federal anti-retaliation rule for employees who report unsafe conditions. Patients and nurses gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor — 19 House members in all — was a Democrat, no Republican signed on, and the bill never got far enough for a recorded vote.

industries.note: Hospitals, psychiatric hospitals, ambulatory surgical centers, rural clinics, and dialysis facilities would have had to publish per-shift staffing, mortality, and complication data as a condition of Medicare participation, and face fines for retaliating against whistleblowers. Facilities with poor staffing had the most to lose from that exposure.

industries.industry: Nursing home and long-term care operators
industries.note: Skilled nursing facilities would have filed quarterly, audited staffing reports and been ranked by percentile in their state on a public staffing quality measure. The bill's own findings cite CMS research linking low nursing home staffing to pressure sores, infections, and weight loss, so the disclosures were aimed squarely at the industry's weakest performers.

Accrediting organizations whose standards are deemed to satisfy Medicare rules would have had their complaint data and investigation findings made public, reducing the privacy their review process currently enjoys, though they face no penalties.
